methodology: Confirmed All comments, expanded the 13 replies under 江柏漢 and replies under 宮屏惠, Richard Lee and 張振豪, and continued to the end of the list. Fifty-nine unique source IDs matched the displayed count. A reply appearing during the reading process was included; the completion time is recorded, and this was not an atomic snapshot.
coverageNote: Only publicly loadable content at completion is covered. Deleted, hidden, blocked or permission-restricted historical comments cannot be recovered. The original post’s 18-comment capture is recorded separately.
relationshipNote: Replies to top-level comments follow platform labels. An exact nested parent link is supplied only when the displayed recipient and earlier visible comments uniquely match. Three ambiguous replies retain recipient names and candidate lists. Replies follow their root in time order; indentation level 2 means a reply to a reply, not an exact full chain length.
timeNote: Times follow Facebook’s display in Taiwan time (UTC+8), to the minute, without invented seconds. Edited indicators are not complete revision histories.
reactionNote: “Liked by author” is a captured interface state, not agreement with every point. Reactions do not establish public opinion, translation quality or mobilization.

items.author: 江柏漢
items.title: Questioning whether public discussion amounts to public shaming
paragraphs: 江柏漢 says he has long read the author’s technical articles, then questions publishing a dispute after a rejected PR, seeing an element of public shaming. He argues that joining a project means following its rules and considering maintainers’ feelings, while also affirming the value of a willingness to contribute.

items.author: 宮屏惠
items.title: Suggesting a brief agreement to end an argument
paragraphs: 宮屏惠 suggests responding in English that the other party is right. She does not elaborate on the PR or translation quality.

items.author: Roga Lin
items.title: Recognizing years of sharing and community work
paragraphs: Roga Lin praises the author’s sustained sharing of knowledge and community work over many years, saying that readers including himself have quietly supported him.

items.author: Watson Chen
items.title: Focusing on understanding and checking AI output
paragraphs: Watson Chen argues that AI use alone should not disqualify work if the person understands and checks the output. His criticism targets generation without quality control. This is a view about responsibility, not a review of this translation.

items.author: 劉育維
items.title: Connecting the post’s advice with personal difficulties
paragraphs: 劉育維 says recent problems have troubled him and that the post’s advice about trusting one’s efforts and not needing to persuade everyone helped him find some answers. He expresses mutual encouragement.

items.author: Tonny Chiu
items.title: Joking about course sales
paragraphs: Tonny Chiu jokes that the author already has ample sales, echoing the post’s suggestion that readers need not add more encouragement.

items.author: Locutus Cardassia
items.title: Mentioning a fork as an option when people disagree
paragraphs: Locutus Cardassia jokingly notes that a common open-source option is to fork when people disagree. This proposes a way to continue work, rather than claiming a new project has been established here.

items.author: 陳大衛
items.title: Using vulgar language to criticize mockers
paragraphs: 陳大衛 uses vulgar language to generalize about people he sees as seeking amusement at others’ expense and speculates about their lives or mental state. He says good deeds do not require approval and jokes that his own barbs can serve as reminders. His generalizations about others’ circumstances are unsupported assessments.

items.author: 大魔術熊貓工程師
items.title: Supporting the protection of personal enthusiasm
paragraphs: 大魔術熊貓工程師 agrees with attending to one’s feelings and sees leaving negative interactions when necessary as a way to protect enthusiasm for open source.

items.author: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: The author admits not expecting the maintainer to see Facebook
paragraphs: Responding to 江柏漢, the author accepts that this was his problem. He says he would not have written in the same way if the other party spoke Chinese, and wrote more freely because he did not expect the Facebook post to be read. He still sees room for discussion and asks whether he should simply keep the peace. This account of his expectations and choices does not independently establish every allegation about mobilization or intent.

items.author: Lxs Artmily
items.title: Characterizing the post as venting about an experience
paragraphs: Lxs Artmily disagrees with calling it public shaming and sees the author as publicly venting about something that happened to him.

items.author: 王哲驊
items.title: Opposing an automatic label of public shaming
paragraphs: 王哲驊 argues that raising a discussion should be allowed. Provided it is not fabricated, merely describing what happened should not automatically be called public shaming. He objects to using that label to restrict public expression.

items.author: Sam Lin
items.title: Allowing both public discussion and maintainer discretion
paragraphs: Sam Lin refers to a statement by Linus and argues that people may discuss public projects in their own spaces; interactions also have a public dimension when maintainers accept others’ contributions. He simultaneously acknowledges maintainer discretion. No link to the referenced Linus post is provided, so it is not equated with the mailing-list message checked elsewhere in this chronicle.

items.author: 江柏漢
items.replyToAuthor: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: Calling rejected PRs a normal part of open source
paragraphs: Replying to the author, 江柏漢 says rejected PRs are an ordinary part of open source, with nothing exceptional about that outcome.

items.author: 江柏漢
items.replyToAuthor: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: Affirming the intention to contribute and encouraging continued work
paragraphs: 江柏漢 adds that people’s willingness to help is an important community asset and hopes the author will continue supporting the community and software industry.

items.author: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: The author says the surprise was being called AI slop
paragraphs: The author says he was polite on GitHub, did not intend to argue and has had many PRs rejected before. Being called AI slop for the first time was the surprise. He describes the Facebook post as venting, says he did not intend an escalation and again says he did not expect the maintainer to read it. These remain his descriptions of intent and tone.
notes: The page gives only the recipient’s name, and this thread contains several earlier replies by that person. An exact parent comment ID cannot be uniquely identified. Replies are grouped under the known top-level comment without guessing the precise parent.

items.author: Lxs Artmily
items.replyToAuthor: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: Locating the complaint in the tone of rejection
paragraphs: Lxs Artmily sees the original issue as whether to accept AI translation but criticizes the maintainer’s impolite wording. In vulgar, joking language, he considers that sufficient reason to vent publicly.
notes: The page gives only the recipient’s name, and this thread contains several earlier replies by that person. An exact parent comment ID cannot be uniquely identified. Replies are grouped under the known top-level comment without guessing the precise parent.

items.author: 林博仁
items.replyToAuthor: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: Recommending human editing of generated interactions
paragraphs: 林博仁 argues against directly using AI tools to interact with maintainers unless a project explicitly permits it. He sees generated signals in the issue and PR descriptions, rather than the diff, as the trigger, potentially giving the impression of a human proxy mass-submitting low-quality agent output. Even if files are created automatically, he recommends removing unnecessary explanation, observing interaction conventions and possibly documenting them as a skill. His account of the maintainer’s perception is an interpretation.
notes: The page gives only the recipient’s name, and this thread contains several earlier replies by that person. An exact parent comment ID cannot be uniquely identified. Replies are grouped under the known top-level comment without guessing the precise parent.

items.author: Daniel Chen
items.title: Requesting an advance policy and criticizing the rejection’s tone
paragraphs: Daniel Chen argues that maintainers also have responsibilities: with AI assistance common, a strong objection should be communicated beforehand. He acknowledges generated-writing signals but personally finds the motivation and changes clear and fairly concise, apart from the questionable explanation for missing screenshots. He also criticizes the lack of a reply to the contributor’s explanation, followed by harsher wording elsewhere. This differs from 林博仁’s assessment of the same description.

items.author: Frank Sung
items.title: Emphasizing the right to reject and respect for stated requirements
paragraphs: Frank Sung argues that responsibility for decisions includes a maintainer’s right to reject in any tone. He frames the issue as respect and criticizes using AI again to rewrite text as one’s own after being told no AI. His accusations of pretending and his judgments about attitude are not independently verified facts.
notes: The author openly acknowledged AI assistance in #97 and again on Facebook. Another commenter’s accusation alone cannot establish deliberate deception.

items.author: Daniel Chen
items.title: Acknowledging the right to reject while asking for fuller context
paragraphs: Replying to Frank Sung, Daniel Chen says he never denied the maintainer’s right to reject, believes Frank has not fully understood the events and asks him to learn the context first. This makes the distinction between the right to reject and how rejection is communicated more explicit.

items.author: Keio Kwan
items.title: Agreeing with the brief-response strategy
paragraphs: Keio Kwan replies to 宮屏惠 with complete agreement and a one-hundred-percent emoji.

items.author: 許友財
items.title: Quoting a classical saying about perseverance
paragraphs: 許友財 quotes a classical saying to express determination after self-reflection. No additional event or technical evidence is offered.

items.author: Anderson A. Thomas
items.title: A Buddhist image of steadiness amid outside judgment
paragraphs: Anderson A. Thomas locates the problem in people’s prejudice toward tools. He uses the Buddhist image of remaining unmoved by the eight winds to describe resilience to judgment, and likens the original motivation for open source to a lamp illuminating the path. These are metaphors and value judgments.

items.author: Bevis Leong
items.title: A reader from Macau thanks the author
paragraphs: Bevis Leong identifies himself as a reader from Macau and thanks the author for sharing over the years, saying he has benefited greatly.

items.author: Sheng Lee
items.title: Expressing support through a recent class experience
paragraphs: Sheng Lee expresses continued support and says he learned a great deal in a recent class. This is a personal account.

items.author: Yang Yung Ling
items.title: Distinguishing a sound action from the way it is presented
paragraphs: Yang Yung Ling distinguishes doing the right thing from adopting the right manner and says events have causes. The brief comment does not specify a particular action or assign responsibility to one side.

items.author: 陳嘉慶
items.title: Hoping for future articles about Linux
paragraphs: 陳嘉慶 builds on the author’s macOS experience and hopes he will try Linux and share his experience. This is a related exchange, not a review of the PR.

items.author: 柯盛達
items.title: Recalling learning about development tools through the author’s teaching
paragraphs: 柯盛達 thanks the author’s teaching and sharing. He recalls searching for VS Code settings, discovering Copilot through the author’s GitHub teaching, and later using Claude and Codex. Although he has seen fewer articles recently, he remains grateful for that help.

items.author: 陳盛晃
items.title: Saying course enrollment is a form of support
paragraphs: 陳盛晃 says he enrolled in every class as a form of paid support. This chronicle has not checked enrollment or transaction records.

items.author: Richard Lee
items.title: Comparing published work with a family heirloom
paragraphs: Richard Lee suggests treating the work as an heirloom for later generations and worrying less about others’ opinions. This prompts a joking exchange about whether the next generation will appreciate it.

items.author: Horst Kan
items.title: Prioritizing personal enjoyment
paragraphs: Horst Kan says enjoying the work oneself is enough and that other people’s opinions need not weigh too heavily.

items.author: 賴禹翰
items.title: Taking useful criticism while treating the rest as noise
paragraphs: 賴禹翰 recommends returning to the original enjoyment of the work and accepting that some will need it and others will dislike it. Suggestions for improvement can be taken from negative comments; the rest need not be internalized. He also thanks the author for public resources.

items.author: 莊念迪
items.title: Sharing experience of PRs left unanswered
paragraphs: 莊念迪 says some of his PRs received no maintainer response while most were merged, adding a personal example of differing open-source outcomes.

items.author: 張小白
items.title: Seeing shortcomings in old work as evidence of growth
paragraphs: 張小白 says technology changes quickly and he often dislikes his earlier work. Being able to recognize its shortcomings now, he suggests, reflects personal progress.

items.author: 魏吉彥
items.title: Encouragement to keep going
paragraphs: 魏吉彥 offers encouragement and urges the author to continue, without developing an argument about the incident.

items.author: Tang Jung Kui
items.title: Learning new information from the author’s posts
paragraphs: Tang Jung Kui says the author’s sharing introduced him to much new information.

items.author: Eric Chang
items.title: Praising openness and sustained contributions
paragraphs: Eric Chang expresses respect for the author’s openness in this post and his sustained sharing.

items.author: 林雨蒼
items.title: A brief thank-you for the contributions
paragraphs: 林雨蒼 thanks the author for his contributions without further comment on this PR.

items.author: Lo Miller
items.title: A brief “come on” remark with unclear tone
paragraphs: Lo Miller leaves a short phrase that could be rendered as “come on, okay?” The comment offers no further context; this chronicle does not decide whether it is encouragement or sarcasm.

items.author: Jun-Yuan Yan
items.title: Encouraging persistence in what one believes is right
paragraphs: Jun-Yuan Yan encourages continuing to do what one believes is right, with an encouraging emoji.

items.author: Kavin Wang
items.title: Crediting development experience with better use of AI
paragraphs: Kavin Wang questions the insistence on rejection and argues that the author’s development experience makes his use of AI different from that of an average user. Praise of personal ability does not substitute for checking this translation paragraph by paragraph.

items.author: 張振豪
items.title: Asking about a live class
paragraphs: 張振豪 asks whether the author might offer a live class, prompting the subsequent course-information reply.

items.author: 陳永富
items.title: Recalling helpful solutions as a beginner
paragraphs: 陳永富 says he sought the author’s solutions when starting out and benefited from them.

items.author: Ryan Pan
items.title: Responding with a cartoon GIF containing “good”
paragraphs: Ryan Pan attaches an animated cartoon containing the word good, without a written argument about the incident. The GIF was inspected; the image alone does not establish his position on every disputed point.

items.author: 楊禮峰
items.title: Recommending time for worthwhile things
paragraphs: 楊禮峰 suggests spending life on worthwhile things and letting an unpleasant incident pass rather than allowing it to occupy one’s thoughts indefinitely.

items.author: Jacey Taavi
items.title: Criticizing both a sweeping rejection and a mixed-scope PR
paragraphs: Jacey Taavi finds the rejection too sweeping while also seeing unnecessary material in the PR. He recommends using the author’s experience to tidy it before resubmitting and links the diff. He does not simply endorse one side or list every change he considers unnecessary.
notes: The commenter refers to the TOML author. The verifiable rejecting account is project member arp242; this does not establish involvement by TOML’s founder. The PR includes shared-template and code changes beyond translated prose, but calling particular changes unnecessary remains the commenter’s assessment.

items.author: 巴農索
items.title: Questioning the other party’s ability to recognize AI writing
paragraphs: 巴農索 negatively judges the other party as so preoccupied with AI that human expression becomes unrecognizable. This is an assessment, not a verified ability or psychological condition.

items.author: 李奎翰
items.title: Comparing the reaction with insults dating back to BBS culture
paragraphs: 李奎翰 says online insults existed in the BBS era and are more common now, generalizing about younger people dismissing things they have not experienced. He extends the point with a joke about someone denying BBS existed, without offering a review of this translation.

items.author: Albert Chang
items.title: A disparaging remark aimed at critics
paragraphs: Albert Chang disparagingly suggests that the critic plainly did not grow up reading the author’s articles. This is a short judgment directed at critics.

items.author: C-j Kang
items.title: Finding the articles useful
paragraphs: C-j Kang thanks the author for sharing and says the articles are useful to him.

items.author: 黃仁靖
items.title: Saying people already know the author
paragraphs: 黃仁靖 briefly says that everyone knows the author, without specifying a position on the incident.

items.author: 王品傑
items.title: Valuing explanations in plain language
paragraphs: 王品傑 praises the author for making the same material easier to understand and reducing the burden of learning. He sees plain-language teaching as an important part of the author’s value.

items.author: Kai-hsiang Wang
items.title: Valuing the willingness to share
paragraphs: Kai-hsiang Wang says the willingness to share is itself worthy of appreciation.

items.author: John Yeung
items.title: An analogy with good gaming performance being mistaken for cheating
paragraphs: John Yeung recalls being accused of cheating in shooting games when his reactions were fast, comparing that with the author being accused of using AI because of his ability. This is the commenter’s analogy: the author publicly acknowledged AI assistance, so it cannot support rewriting the case as involving no AI use.

items.author: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: The author jokes that descendants may not appreciate his work
paragraphs: Replying to the heirloom metaphor, the author jokes self-deprecatingly that the next generation may not appreciate what he leaves behind. This does not establish what actual family members will think in the future.

items.author: Richard Lee
items.replyToAuthor: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: Leaving the next generation’s opinion to that generation
paragraphs: Richard Lee replies that the next generation can decide its own opinion; the present generation can first find satisfaction in its work.

items.author: Will 保哥的技術交流中心
items.title: The author supplies information about a live class
paragraphs: Replying to 張振豪, the author says a class will take place that Friday and includes a course link and promotional image. This records a historical exchange, not a guarantee of current availability or an enrollment recommendation.

items.author: Daniel Chen
items.title: Again separating rejection rights, tone and contribution guidelines
paragraphs: Daniel Chen again acknowledges that maintainers can reject in any tone but argues that extreme unfriendliness drives contributors away. He wants contribution guidelines to state boundaries in advance to reduce conflict. This reply appeared during the capture process and was included in the completed inventory.
